initial_assessment: Daniel Sample is a 34-year-old man (born 1992-06-01) with about one week of headache and vomiting and ECOG performance status 2, recorded 2026-10-16. Contrast MRI on 2026-10-17 shows a well-circumscribed, lobulated, extra-axial/cortically based left frontal mass measuring 4.2 x 3.5 x 3.0 cm, and a separate discrete 5 mm lobulated nodule on the posterior pial surface of the cord at C6 with intense uniform enhancement; cord caliber is otherwise normal. Stereotactic needle biopsy of the frontal mass on 2026-10-19 is reported only as suggestive of an intracranial mesenchymal tumor with spinal drop metastasis, and the report states that the final histologic and molecular entity is not established on the current material. Both conditions remain verificationStatus provisional and are coded as neoplasms of uncertain behavior (ICD-10-CM D43.0 supratentorial brain; D43.4 spinal cord). The C6 nodule is imaging-suspected and has not been biopsied. This is not a confirmed diagnosis, grade, or molecular entity, and it is not a basis for disease-directed therapy.
diagnostic_confirmation_and_staging: The immediate diagnostic task is an integrated neuropathology review of the stereotactic specimen, not assignment of a subtype. Needed results are a full immunohistochemical panel directed at the intracranial mesenchymal differential, DNA methylation profiling/classifier, RNA-based fusion testing, and a targeted DNA sequencing panel. Findings that would change management, and that are not in the chart, include a definitive WHO entity and grade; a defining fusion or mutation (for example FET::CREB, NAB2::STAT6, DICER1, CIC rearrangement, or another fusion-defined sarcoma); evidence that this is metastasis from an extracranial sarcoma rather than a primary CNS tumor; and tissue adequacy versus a non-diagnostic or insufficient sample that would require further sampling rather than empiric treatment. No such molecular or IHC results are present. Staging already includes contrast brain MRI and contrast MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine, but the spine conclusion documents only the C6 nodule, so an explicit statement on the remainder of the neuraxis is required. Complete systemic staging (chest, abdomen, and pelvis; PET only if metastatic sarcoma remains in the differential) before any disease-directed plan. Do not label the C6 lesion a drop metastasis until radiology and pathology agree it is related; cord biopsy is not the first step and would be considered only if it uniquely changes the diagnosis and can be done safely. CSF sampling is deferred until imaging review excludes mass effect or obstruction.
immediate_management_plan: Short-horizon plan is diagnostic confirmation, safe staging, symptom control, and multidisciplinary review. Disease-directed chemotherapy and definitive radiotherapy are deferred until entity, WHO grade, extent, and resectability are established; no regimen is selected. Same-day neurosurgical and neuroradiology review should determine edema, shift, hydrocephalus, eloquent-cortex and vascular relationships, and whether resection, rather than the completed needle biopsy, is needed for both decompression and adequate tissue. Symptom control is guided by that review: treat headache and vomiting with analgesia and antiemetics; use corticosteroids only if vasogenic edema or mass effect is confirmed; use antiseizure medication only for witnessed seizures or a documented perioperative indication. Observe closely, and admit if headache, vomiting, or neurologic change suggests rising intracranial pressure. Convene neuro-oncology, neurosurgery, neuropathology, and neuroradiology now. Radiation oncology may join for later planning but should not start treatment on a provisional diagnosis. Obtain a formal baseline neurologic examination and hold all disease-directed therapy pending the integrated diagnosis and a documented resectability and staging assessment.
prognosis: No survival figure can be quoted before the diagnosis is confirmed. Prognosis depends on the final entity, WHO grade, local extent and resectability, and whether there is true dissemination. A localized, resectable, lower-grade mesenchymal tumor and a high-grade sarcoma with neuraxial spread would not have the same outlook, and neither scenario is established by a provisional uncertain-behavior code, a limited stereotactic sample, or an unbiopsied 5 mm cord nodule.
